1.18.m: Bhīṣma said: / "Most wondrous is this that I have heard in truth, O Brahmin: / the consecration of Gāyatrī performed there in the assembly,
the opposition of Sāvitrī and the giving of the curse likewise, / and how the goddess was proclaimed in all places by Viṣṇu;
and how Gāyatrī, of fair complexion, was praised by Rudra. / Having heard about the Grandfather, the peerless Self, in detail,
my hair has bristled with joy and my mind has become tranquil; / having heard it, supreme delight and wonder have arisen in me."

The Lord Nārāyaṇa indeed, having performed that supreme
praise of the wife of Brahmā with devotion, and placing her upon the mountain,

Viṣṇu spoke these words that bestow contentment and nourishment:
"O glorious and modest one, you who are the goddess and ruler!"

Only this much, O holy one, has been heard coming forth from your mouth.
What happened there subsequently, and what was performed at that place,

the Lord ought to relate all of that in proper order.
Through hearing it, my body will undoubtedly be purified.

Pulastya said:
While that god, the supreme Lord, was sacrificing at Puṣkara,
listen, O king, to this wonder, just as it was performed formerly.

In the beginning, during that Kṛta age, when the Grandfather was the patron of the sacrifice,
Marīci, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,

and Dakṣa Prajāpati offered obeisance.
Shining beings, adorned with all kinds of ornaments,

and troops of apsarases danced near Viṣṇu, the lord of gods.
Then, with gandharva instruments resounding in the sky,

Tumburu sang along with many gandharvas:
Mahāśruti, Citrasena, Ūrṇāyu, and also Anagha,

Gomāyu, Sūryavarcas, and Somavarcas, O descendant of Kuru,
and along with them Tṛṇāyu, Nandi, and Citraratha,

the thirteenth Śāliśiras, the fourteenth Parjanya,
and here the fifteenth Kali, and the sixteenth Tāraka,

the gandharvas Hāhā and Hūhū, and Haṃsa of great splendour—
these celestial gandharvas sang before the all-pervading Lord.

Likewise, divine apsarases danced before that all-pervading Lord.
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Savitṛ, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, and Bhaga,

Indra, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Parjanya—
these twelve Ādityas, blazing with radiant energy,

and the lords of the gods made obeisance here to the Grandfather.
Mṛgavyādha, Śarva, Nirṛti of great renown,

Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, Aparājita,
Bhava, Viśveśvara, and Kapardin, O ruler of people,

Sthāṇu, and the lordly Bhaga—the Rudras stood there;
the two Aśvins, the eight Vasus, and the mighty Maruts,

the Viśvedevas and the Sādhyas stood before him with joined palms;
and the great nāgas beginning with Śeṣa, headed by Vāsuki,

Kāśyapa, Kambala, and the mighty Takṣaka—
these great-souled nāgas stood before him with joined palms.

Tārkṣya, Ariṣṭanemi, the mighty Garuḍa,
Vāruṇi, and Āruṇi—the sons of Vinatā stood in attendance.

The Lord Nārāyaṇa himself, possessing realms and endowed with glory,
having arrived along with all the great sages, addressed the teacher of the world:

"By you this entire [universe] is pervaded; by you it has been created, O Lord of the world.
Therefore you are the Lord of the worlds. O lotus-born one, obeisance to you!

Whatever is to be done here by me, command that work."
Thus spoke the sovereign Lord, together with the divine seers,

having bowed to Brahmā, the lord of gods, whose birth is unmanifest.
And Brahmā, remaining there, illuminated the directions with his splendour,

covered with the hair of the Śrīvatsa, shining with a golden cord,
resembling the divine seers, glorious, the self-existent creator of beings,

with pure hair, broad-chested, the lord consisting of all radiant energy,
who is the path for those of virtuous conduct, and an impassable way for evil-doers,

whom the great-souled masters of yoga know as the highest realm,
whose sovereign power is eightfold, whom they call the best of gods,

reaching whom, the eternal one, the self-restrained brāhmaṇas who desire liberation
and are absorbed in yoga are freed from birth and death,

which those dwelling in all hermits' stages call austerity,
practising it repeatedly, restricted in food, undertaking difficult vows,

who is called Ananta among the serpents by all practitioners of yoga,
thousand-headed, red-eyed, by the unsurpassed beings headed by Śeṣa,

who is worshipped as sacrifice by the best of brāhmaṇas desirous of heaven,
having courses in various places, glorious, the one unsurpassed sage,

which god the knower recognizes as the bestower of the sacrificial portion,
whose eyes are the bull, fire, the sun, and the moon, the god whose body is space—

to that god we resort, O Lord, seeking shelter,
the protector, the refuge, the god who is the source of the origin of all gods,

the creator of the seers and of the worlds, the lord of gods,
for the pleasure of the gods and for the maintenance of the entire world,

by whom the fitting ancestral oblation for the ancestors and the supreme oblation for the gods
were instituted—to that best of gods we bow down."

Indeed, as the god, the supreme Lord, was sacrificing with the triple fire,
just as creation was accomplished formerly, so again the creation of the sacrifice was done.

Likewise, even Brahmā, attended upon by Ananta
who causes the preservation of the worlds, the venerable Lord, aged and yet wise,

the Grandfather, whose self is inconceivable, went to the sacrificial enclosure,
filled with priests rich in wealth and guarded by members of the assembly.

Then, with his bow taken up by powerful Viṣṇu,
the kings of the daityas and dānavas and hosts of rākṣasas stood [at bay].

By himself he swiftly contemplated his own self;
having contemplated the sacrifice in accordance with reality, the eternal Sacrifice,

the Lord arranged for the formal selection of the sacrificial priests there;
and the priests, beginning with Bhṛgu, skilled in the rites of the sacrifice,

recited the sacred syllable spoken by the foremost Ṛgvedic priests;
those best of sages listened as the rite was performed in extended detail there.

Through the sacrificial science, Vedic science, and [the expertise] of knowers of the pada and krama texts,
[the ground] resounded with the loud chanting of the supreme seers.

By the twice-born knowers of the sacrificial layout and scholars of phonetics,
knowers of the derivation and meaning of words, proficient in all branches of learning,

knowers of Mīmāṃsā and syllogistic statements, various discussions were conducted at the opening;
and there, here and there, O king of kings, self-controlled men of strict vows

beheld the foremost brāhmaṇas intent upon silent recitation and oblations into the fire.
Brahmā, the Grandfather of the world, stood upon that sacrificial ground,

the glorious teacher of gods and asuras, served by gods and asuras;
and there the lords of creatures worshipped him, the Lord:

Dakṣa, Vasiṣṭha, Pulaha, and the best of the twice-born Marīci,
Aṅgiras, Bhṛgu, Atri, Gautama, and Nārada.

The existing space, the intermediate region, wind, fire, water, and earth;
sound, touch, form, taste, and also smell;

the transformed and transformation, and whatever other great cause there is;
and the four Vedas, named Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan,

accompanied by grammar, phonetics, etymology, ritual codes, and metre,
Āyurveda, the science of archery, Mīmāṃsā, and mathematics,

along with the knowledge of elephants and horses, and endowed with legendary history—
all the Vedas, adorned with these auxiliary and subordinate limbs,

worshipped the great-souled Grandfather along with the sacred syllable Oṃ;
austerity, the sacrificial rites, intention, and breath,

these and many others attended upon the Grandfather:
wealth, righteousness, desire, aversion, and ever-present joy,

Śukra, Bṛhaspati, Saṃvarta, Budha,
Śanaiścara, Rāhu, and likewise all the planets.
The Maruts, Viśvakarman, and the ancestors, O descendant of Bharata, / and the Sun and the Moon worship Brahmā.
Gāyatrī who carries across misfortune, sevenfold Speech, / and all the syllables, as well as the lunar mansions,
the commentaries, all the treatises in embodied form, O ruler of the people, / moments, instants, and hours, as well as day and night,
fortnights, months, and all the sacrifices— / [all these] worship the great-souled Brahmā along with the deities.
And other foremost goddesses: Modesty, Fame, and Splendor, / Radiance, Fortitude, Forbearance, Prosperity, Conduct, Knowledge, and Intelligence,
Revelation, Tradition, as well as Patience, Peace, Nourishment, and Action, / and all the celestial apsarases skilled in dance and song,
all those divine mothers wait upon Brahmā. / Vipracitti, Śivi, Śaṅku, and Ayaḥśaṅku,
Vegavat, Ketumat, Ugra, Sogrovyagra the great asura, / Parigha, Puṣkara, Sāmba, and Aśvapati,

Then Prahlāda, Bali, Kumbha, Saṃhrāda, Gaganapriya,
Anuhrāda, Hari, Hara, Varāha, Kuśa, and Raja.
Yonibhakṣa, Vṛṣaparvan, Liṅgabhakṣa, and Vaikuru, / Niḥprabha, Saprabha, Śrīmat, and Nirudara,
Ekacakra, Mahācakra, Dvicakra, Kulasaṃbhava, / Śarabha, Śalabha, Krapatha, Krāpatha, and Kratha,
Bṛhadvānti, Mahājihva, Śaṅkukarṇa, Mahādhvani, / Dīrghajihva, Arkanayana, Mṛḍakāya, Mṛḍapriya,
Vāyu, Gariṣṭha, Namuci, Śambara, Vijvara, Vibhu, / Viṣvaksena, Candrahartṛ, and Krodhavardhana,
Kālaka, Kalakānta, Kuṇḍada who loves battle, / Gariṣṭha, Variṣṭha, Pralamba, Naraka, Pṛthu,
Indratāpana, Vātāpi, Ketumat proud in strength, / Asiloman, Suloman, Bāṣkali, Pramada, Mada,
Sṛgālavadana, Keśin, Śarada, / Ekākṣa, Rāhu, Vṛtra, and Krodhavimokṣaṇa—
these and many other Dānavas who swell with power / attended upon Brahmā, and then spoke this word:
"We were created by you, O Lord; by you indeed the three worlds / were given to us, O best of the boons of gods, and we were made superior to the gods.
O Lord, what shall we do here in your sacrifice, O grandfather? / Tell what is beneficial to us; we are capable of carrying out the task.
What [use] to you are these wretched deities born from the womb of Aditi, / who are always being struck down and constantly defeated?
You are the grandfather of all of us together with the deities. / And when your sacrifice is concluded, between the deities and us
hostility over sovereignty will occur again, without a doubt. / Now we will watch, united with all the Dānavas."
Pulastya said: / Hearing their arrogant words, the divine Janārdana, / renowned, spoke this to Śambhu along with Śakra:
"The foremost among the sons of Danu have arrived to cause an obstacle, O Rudra! / They were invited by Brahmā, and here they are striving to cause an obstacle.
We must show patience until the sacrifice is concluded. / But when this sacrifice is completed, battle must be waged by the gods.
You must act, O lord, so that the earth becomes free of Dānavas, / and together with me, here, for the victory of Śakra.
The Maruts have been appointed as the attendants of the twice-born. / Taking whatever wealth the Dānavas have, we sacrifice with that.
When the brāhmaṇas and the distressed people have arrived here, / we will spend that [wealth] on them, reducing [the Dānavas] to the status of servants."
As he was speaking thus to Viṣṇu, Brahmā spoke words: / "These sons of Danu are angry; they desire to provoke your anger.
You must exercise patience, along with Rudra and the deities. / But when the end of the Kṛta age arrives and the sacrifice has reached completion,
dispatched by me, all of you and these foremost of Danu's sons / must at that very time make either peace or war."
Pulastya said: / The lord Brahmā himself spoke again to those Dānavas: / "There should be no conflict here with the Dānavas at my sacrifice in any way.
Abide in a friendly disposition and continuously in our work." / The Dānavas said: / "We shall do all this, your instruction, O grandfather.
The gods are our younger brothers; let there be no fear for them." / Pulastya said: / Hearing this then from them, the grandfather was deeply pleased.
While they remained for a moment, ten million sages arrived, / having heard of the grandfather's sacrifice. Keśava performed their worship.
The god who wields the Pināka then gave them seats. / Commanded by Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha offered them the guest-water.
Having given the cow and the guest-water, and asked about their unfailing welfare, / he assigned them quarters at Puṣkara and said, "Please remain here."
Then all those sages wearing matted hair and black-antelope skins / graced that best of lakes, like the gods adorning the Gaṅgā.
Some had shaved heads, some wore ochre robes, and others had long beards; / some had sparse teeth, and others had flattened eyes;
some had large, emaciated bellies, and others had squinting eyes; / some had long ears, some had deformed ears, and others had torn ears;
some had long foreheads, some had broad foreheads, and they were enveloped only in sinews and skin; / and their bellies were sunken—those sages of purified soul.
Seeing the holy ford of Puṣkara shining brightly on all sides, / drawn by longing for the sacred ford, O tiger among men, they settled upon its bank.
There were the great-souled Vālakhilyas, others who bruised their grain with stones, / others who used their teeth as a mortar, and others who washed [all they had] clean;
others fed on air, lived on water, or lived on fallen leaves, / observant of various disciplines, and sleeping upon bare ground.
Beholding their faces in this lake, in an instant their countenances became beautiful. / Wondering "What is this?", they looked at one another.
"In this holy ford, by the seeing of the face beauty of the face is attained here!" / Calling it "Face-Beholding" (Mukhadarśana), the ascetics
bathed and observed their disciplines, and they immediately became handsome. / They appeared like sons of gods, endowed with incomparable qualities.
Shining bright, O best of men, all those forest-dwellers stood; / with just their sacred thread, they quickly shared the holy ford.
Offering oblations in the sacred fire-altars, they performed various rites, / reflecting [upon the ford], O king of kings, their sins burned away through austerity:
"We shall go to no other holy ford; this lake is foremost in seniority." / Thus the twice-born named it Senior Puṣkara (Jyeṣṭhapuṣkara).
Seeing many hunchbacks standing there near the holy ford, / the people who had assembled there were filled with wonder.
Having given gifts and various vessels to the twice-born, / hearing of the eastern Sarasvatī, the twice-born came, desiring to bathe.
The Sarasvatī, best of holy waters, was frequented by various flocks of birds, / [and lined] with jujube, inguda, kāśmarya, plakṣa, aśvattha, and vibhītaka trees,
with pauloma, palāśa, karīra, and pīlu trees, / and with dhanvana and syandana trees growing beside the holy waters of the Sarasvatī.
[The river was] adorned with wood-apples, oleanders, bilvas, and āmlātakas, / and with clumps of atimuktaka and pārijāta trees,
abounding in groves of kadambas, delighting all creatures; / and frequented by highest ascetics who fed on air, water, fruits, and fallen leaves, and by those who use teeth as mortars,
as well as by foremost sages who use stones as pestles, / resounding with the chanting of their Vedic recitations, and crowded with hundreds of herds of deer;
and exceedingly beautified by those devoted to non-violence and highest righteousness. / Known as Suprabhā, Kāñcanā, Prācī, Nandā, and Viśālakā,
the river flows there in Puṣkara in five streams, / when Pitāmaha's sacrificial gathering was taking place upon the earth.
When the sacrificial arena was spread out, and the twice-born and others had been welcomed, / with extensive shouts of 'auspicious day!' and with observances for the gods,
and when the gods were engaged in that ritual of the sacrifice, / and Pitāmaha, O great king, had taken the sacrificial consecration,
as he was offering the sacrifice that fulfills every desire, / objects conceived in the mind, promoting righteousness and wealth,
came up there to the twice-born everywhere, O lord of kings; / the celestial Gandharvas sang, and troupes of Apsarases danced.
And they swiftly played heavenly instruments; / the deities were delighted by the perfection of that sacrifice,
and reached the highest astonishment—what then of human beings? / When the sacrifice was proceeding thus, with Pitāmaha residing in Puṣkara,
the pleased ṛṣis then spoke to Sarasvatī, O Bhīṣma: / 'You are Sarasvatī by name, O lord of kings, and Suprabhā by name.'
Seeing Sarasvatī endowed with swift speed, / illuminating Pitāmaha and his sacrifice, all those sages held it in high regard.
Thus this best of rivers, Sarasvatī, / arose in Puṣkara for the sake of Pitāmaha and for the delight of the wise.
Making holy things yet holier, five-streamed is Sarasvatī, / Suprabhā by name, O lord of kings, and also named Sarasvatī.
Where those tranquil sages recited various Vedic studies, / those ṛṣis, having gathered there, remembered Sarasvatī.
Meditated upon by the sages performing the sacrificial session, the illustrious, / great river, pleased by their devotion, took her stand flowing toward the eastern direction.
Flowing eastward, she is named Prācī, the Sarasvatī worshipped by sages. / Hear another supreme marvel on earth, O great king:
The brāhmaṇa Maṅkaṇaka was wounded by the tip of a kuśa grass, so we have heard; / from the wound on his hand, O king, vegetable juice indeed flowed.
Seeing that vegetable juice, he was seized with joy and began to dance; / then, while he was dancing, the immovable and the movable creation,
the entire world began to dance, bewildered by his splendor. / By the gods headed by Śakra, O king, and by ṛṣis rich in ascetic power,
Brahmā was petitioned there: 'Act so that he does not dance.' / Commanded by Brahmā for the sake of the ṛṣi, O king,
[Rudra said:] 'You must speak in such a way, O terrible one, that he will not dance.' / Rudra, having gone and seen the sage deeply seized with joy, [said:]
'O best of brāhmaṇas, why do you dance? / For as you dance, the entire universe dances.'
Restrained by him, that best of sages said as he danced: / The sage said: / 'Do you not see, O god, that vegetable juice flows from my hand?
Seeing that, I have begun to dance, filled with great joy.' / Laughing, the god said to that sage who was bewildered by passion:
'I do not feel any astonishment here, O brāhmaṇa; look at me.' / When spoken to thus by Mahādeva, O Kaurava,
the best of sages wondered: 'Who is this by whom I have been forbidden?' / Then, O lord of kings, with the tip of his finger his own thumb was struck.
Thereupon ash, white as snow, came out from the wound, O king; / seeing that, he felt ashamed, and falling at his feet, he said:
'I consider no other god greater than Rudra; / you are the goal of the moving and unmoving universe, O bearer of the trident!
Wise men say that all this has been created by you; / everything enters into you alone again at the end of the cosmic age.
Even the gods cannot know you; how then could I? / In you are seen all the gods, even Brahmā and the rest.
You are everything, the agent and the instigator of all gods; / by your grace all the deities here become free from fear.'
Having praised Mahādeva thus, the bowed sage said: / 'O Lord, by your favor let not my ascetic power diminish here.'
Then the god, his mind pleased, said again to that sage: / 'O brāhmaṇa, let your ascetic power increase a thousandfold by my grace!
I will always dwell here in Prācī together with you; / Sarasvatī is exceedingly holy, especially in this sacred place.
Nothing is difficult for him to attain in this world or the next / who casts off his own body on the northern bank of Sarasvatī.
He who is devoted to recitation on the bank of Prācī does not die again here; / having bathed, he will obtain the abundant fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Emaciating his body through observances and fasts, / the ascetic taking only water, consuming only wind, or eating only leaves,
and sleeping on bare ground, and whatever other various observances there are— / whatever best of twice-born performs those observances and vows,
his body purified, goes to the supreme abode of Brahmā. / But in that holy place, by those who give gold even the size of a sesamum seed,
it becomes equal to the gift of Mount Meru; so Prajāpati said formerly. / Moreover, the mortals who perform an ancestral rite in that holy place,
those men will go to heaven along with twenty-one generations of their family. / The holy place brings fortune to the ancestors, who are satisfied by a single rice-ball;
carried across here by their own son, they will go to the world of Brahmā. / And they desire food no more; they enter upon the path of liberation.
Hear the truth about how Sarasvatī came to be eastward-flowing. / Formerly Sarasvatī was addressed by all the gods together with Vāsava:
'You must go to the shore of the salt ocean in the west; / carrying this submarine fire, deposit it into the ocean.
When this is done, all the gods will become free from fear; / otherwise the submarine fire burns [everything] with its own radiance.
Therefore protect the gods from this fear before long; / be like a mother, O woman of fair hips, granting fearlessness to the gods.'
Thus addressed by all-powerful Viṣṇu, the goddess said: / 'I am not independent; let my father, the self-ruler, be approached.
I am an obedient daughter always carrying out his command, observing vows; / without the instruction of my father, I do not take a single step anywhere.
I will not go; therefore let some other means be thought of, alas!' / Understanding her intention, they assembled and said to Pitāmaha:
'The submarine fire cannot be carried by anyone else, O Pitāmaha, / except by your maiden daughter alone, who has never seen any fault.'
Bringing Sarasvatī and placing the beautiful woman on his lap, / smelling her head with affection, he then said to Sarasvatī:
'And the gods have said to me, O goddess: "Speak to the glorious maiden / that she may carry this submarine fire and cast it into the salt water."'
Hearing that word of her father, like an osprey separated [from her mate], / that maiden, desolate at heart, wept immediately with her father.
Her face, with eyes troubled by tears of grief, looked / like a white, fully opened lotus sprinkled with drops of water.
Seeing her in such a state, the gods, / headed by the Grandfather, all fell under the power of grief.
Stept in to calm her heart, tormented by sorrow, / the Grandfather said to her: "Do not weep; there is no fear for you.
You will attain honor through the majesty of the gods. / Take the fire, daughter, and cast it into the midst of the salt ocean."
Addressed thus, the girl, her eyes clouded with tears, / bowed to the lotus-born [Brahmā] and said, "I will go."
Told again by them and likewise by her father, "Do not fear," / she cast off fear, became gladdened in mind, and prepared to depart.
At the time of her departure, with the sounds of conches and kettledrums / and the auspicious roar of blessings, the world was filled with prosperity.
Clad in white garments, blessed, adorned with white sandalwood paste, / having the fair luster of an autumn lotus, adorned with a necklace of pearls,
with a face like the full moon, her eyes long as lotus petals, / filling the ten directions with the auspicious glory of the lord of the gods,
she went forth from his heart, illuminating the world with her radiance. / As she followed her, the fair-complexioned Gaṅgā was addressed by her:
"Shall I see you again? Where are you going, my friend?" / Being addressed thus, Gaṅgā spoke sweet words:
"Whenever you go toward the eastern direction, auspicious one, you will see me. / Surrounded by the gods, I resort to the sight of you.
Facing northward then, cast off grief, sweet-smiling one! / I face north and am sacred, while you, Sarasvatī, face east.
There, through bathing and giving, one gains the merit of a hundred sacrifices, O virtuous one, / and in giving śrāddha, what is given is ever imperishable to the ancestors.
Those men who perform it will be freed from the three debts; / they will go the path of liberation—on this point there is no doubt."
Then Gaṅgā said to her: "May you be seen again! / Go to your abode, gentle lady; I must be remembered by you, sinless one."
Likewise Yamunā and charming Gāyatrī, / together with Sāvitrī—they all sent their friend away.
Then, taking leave of the gods, becoming a river, / that resolute Sarasvatī arose at the hermitage of Uttaṅka.
Bringing down her body beneath a plakṣa tree, / the illustrious goddess then descended before the eyes of the gods.
That tree had the form of Viṣṇu, praised by all the gods, / always to be served by twice-born men for the sake of fruit, bringing great prosperity.
Spreading out in many branches, it was like another four-faced [Brahmā]. / Of the twice-born men who entered into the crores of huts in its hollows,
diverse utterances are heard, charming the minds of the gods. / Though it is a tree without flowers, it is observed as if blossoming.
With flowers resembling jasmine and campaka, with auspicious parrots clinging to its branches, / and with fragrant ketakī flowers, the excellent river shone.
With kokilas, as if smeared, and as if flowering with frothy foams, / just as Gaṅgā is [held] by Hara, so she was [held] by the plakṣa tree.
Standing in the water there, she then spoke to the god Janārdana: / "Hand over that fire; I will execute the gods' command."
Addressed thus by her, he, Viṣṇu, replied to her then: / "You have no fear of burning; this king of fire must be abandoned by you yourself,
to carry the submarine fire to the western ocean, auspicious one. / Moving thus by degrees, he will reach the waters, fair lady."
Then Govinda, placing that submarine fire into a vessel of gold, / delivered it into the vast expanse of Sarasvatī.
Taking it, the fair-hipped one went facing the west; / through invisibility, that great river arrived at Puṣkara.
On that Maryādā mountain, the stainless river arose / in the vast Puṣkara forest frequented by gods and Siddhas,
where the sacrificial session was attended by the Grandfather. / For the success of the foremost sages, that great river arrived.
Flooding all those kuṇḍas in which oblations / had been made there by Viriñci, she surged forth with her water.
Having arisen thus in that most holy field at Puṣkara, / it is called Puṣkara by Vāyu, the life of the world, because of that filling.
Reaching that sacred field, the holy, great river, / the goddess Sarasvatī, remained, destroying the sins of mortals.
Those of virtuous deeds who see Sarasvatī / present at Puṣkara do not behold that dreadful downfall.
Moreover, that man who should bathe there with devotion / reaches the world of Brahmā and rejoices with Brahmā.
He who gives delightful curds to a brāhmaṇa there, / he too reaches the world of Agni and enjoys splendid pleasures.
Whoever gives an excellent upper garment with devotion to a twice-born man, / he too obtains ten times the fruit of giving good clothes.
The pure-minded man who, having bathed in the Jyeṣṭhakuṇḍa, gratifies the ancestors, / rescues all of them, even from hell.
Reaching the holy Sarasvatī in the sacred field of the Grandfather, / what other holy place would a man pray for? So said the son of Brahmā.
Therefore, whatever fruit a man obtains who has bathed in all holy places, / a mortal who has dipped once in the Jyeṣṭhakuṇḍa would obtain all of that.
What is the use of speaking much here? The field, the holy place, and the auspicious destiny— / he by whom this triad has been attained has attained the supreme destiny.
Whoever, at the proper time, in that field and holy place, having bathed and offered oblations, / gives wealth to a twice-born man, enjoys endless happiness.
In the bright half of the month of Kārttika, in Vaiśākha, [the month] adorned by the moon, / at an eclipse of the moon or the sun, and at that time in Kurujāṅgala—
among the holy places mentioned by the best of sages in these fields, / the Grandfather declared this holy place to be the most sacred.
The man who, on the full-moon day of Kārttika, having bathed in the middle kuṇḍa, / gives wealth to a twice-born man, attains [the merit of] a horse sacrifice.
Likewise, here, having bathed with concentration in the smallest kuṇḍa, / whoever gives to a vipra even a beautiful grain of rice,
that man quickly goes to the delightful world of Agni; / accompanied by twenty-one generations of his family, he enjoys great fruit there.
Therefore, with every effort, a man must make his mind firmly resolute / to go, in order to attain auspicious Puṣkara.
Reaching the Puṣkara forest where Sarasvatī faces east: / Mati, Smṛti, auspicious Prajñā, Medhā, Buddhi, and supreme Dayā—
these are proclaimed to be the six synonyms of Sarasvatī. / From that time onward, wherever this Sarasvatī became eastward-flowing,
even those who, standing on the bank, behold that water present there, / they too obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice; there is no doubt about this.
Or whichever man, having descended there, should perform a bath, / being concentrated, he would indeed become an attendant of Brahmā.
The man who worships the ancestors there, even with vegetables and the like, / he too attains vast pleasures through their very majesty.
Furthermore, those men who perform a śrāddha there according to the rules, / by that deliver the ancestors to heaven, even from grief-giving hell.
The ancestors of that person are satisfied, who, having bathed there, / offers to them purified water mixed with kuśa grass and sesamum seeds.
This is remembered as superior to all tirthas; / therefore this first tirtha is celebrated in the world among tirthas.
It stands as a treasure-trove of play for dharma and liberation, / and joined with the Sarasvatī, it is even more endowed with virtues,
bestowing all four aims: dharma, artha, kāma, and liberation. / Moreover, what men enter the water here to destroy impurity,
the fruit equal to the gift of a cow easily accrues to them; / the wise say it is equal to the gift of gold.
By libation and the offering of rice-balls, even those residing in hells, / the ancestors, carried across by a son, depart to heaven.
At Puṣkara, people who drink water from the Sarasvatī / attain imperishable worlds praised by Brahmā and Viśveśa.
And the Sarasvatī at Puṣkara has become a ladder to heaven; / that great river can be reached by meritorious men.
She was frequented here and there by sages knowing the truth of dharma; / therefore that goddess is pure everywhere and situated on all sides.
At Puṣkara, however, she is especially the purest of the pure; / the holy river Sarasvatī is easily accessible in the world.
She is hard to attain at Kurukṣetra, Prabhāsa, and likewise Puṣkara; / that tirtha is ordained as the foremost of all tirthas on earth,
accomplishing all four: dharma, artha, kāma, and liberation. / Having reached the eastern Sarasvatī, whoever seeks another tirtha
indeed casts away nectar in his hand and desires poison. / In the senior [Puṣkara], she is remembered as Senior Prayāga; in the middle, as Middle [Prayāga].
Then, circumambulating, the discerning man should go to the junior one; / he should bathe in all three and also circumambulate them.
Whoever offers to the ancestors their water accompanied by sesame seeds, / pleased, they give him immeasurable fruit in return.
Having bathed, restrained, one should constantly behold the Grandfather; / in regular order and inverse order, as well as individually and together,
one desiring the world of Brahmā should constantly bathe at Puṣkara. / There are three white peaks and three cascades;
three Puṣkaras are celebrated—we know not the reason there— / the junior, the middle, and the third, Senior Puṣkara,
bearing the names of the peaks, and auspicious cascades. / A man obtains fruit by his intentions for dharma, artha, kāma, and liberation.
Whoever abandons his body there attains liberation without doubt. / Restrained and self-controlled, having bathed in her, he should give to a twice-born
one auspicious cow consecrated with mantras, and he attains worlds that bestow liberation. / What need is there of saying much here? If someone, even at night,
gives wealth to a supplicant after bathing, he enjoys endless happiness. / The best of sages praise the donation of sesame seeds there.
Bathing is always prescribed on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight; / whoever gives a rice-ball here with oil-cake or with jaggery
to the ancestors, having become restrained, goes to the world of the ancestors. / Having reached the Puṣkara forest, from there the Sarasvatī again
went out of sight, and began to go facing westward. / Not far from that Puṣkara, the very beautiful [river]
reached the Kharjūra forest adorned with fruits and flowers. / Having dwelt there in the forest delightful to sages, the goddess again
—overspread with flowers of all seasons, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas— / became the best of rivers named Nandā, celebrated in the three worlds,
abounding in fish, crocodiles, and large fish, filled with clear water. / Sūta said: / Then Devavrata said, “Is she another best of rivers?
This is my curiosity, O brāhmaṇa: how the best of rivers / named Sarasvatī came to be called Nandā, and by what cause.”
When this was spoken, Pulastya began to narrate / to Bhīṣma this ancient account, whence it is remembered as named Nandā:
There was a king, Prabhañjana, who constantly kept the kṣatriya vows; / he set out to slay deer in that forest, being of great might.
Then, in that [forest], he saw a doe standing within a thicket; / he pierced her with a very sharp arrow as she stood before him.
Looking around in all directions and seeing him with bow in hand, / she said: “What have you done, you fool? A terrible deed has been done by you!
I was standing with my face down, offering my breast to my offspring; / out of greed for meat, I have been pierced by force, while fearing nothing.
A king should not kill a deer of such a kind—a nursing mother, one with a hidden fawn, / or one engaged in secret mating—so have I heard before.
I, offering my breast to this offspring, have been slain by you / with an arrow like a thunderbolt, blameless, having come to the forest.
Therefore, O evil-minded one, you too shall attain the state of a carnivorous beast; / in this thorn-filled forest, take the form of a tiger!”
Hearing this pronouncement of a curse, the king, standing before her, / with his senses agitated, folded his hands and addressed the doe:
“I did not think that she was offering her breast to her offspring here; / you were struck through ignorance, O auspicious one! Be gracious through deep composure.
When shall I cast off this tiger-form and attain human form again? / Declare to me, O doe, the release from such a curse!”
When this was said, the doe spoke an auspicious word to him: / “O king, at the end of a hundred years, through a cow that has arrived,
having had a dialogue with Nandā, the end of your curse shall take place.” / Upon the word spoken by the doe, the king then indeed became a tiger,
equipped with claws and fangs as weapons, very terrifying in tiger-form. / There he lived, eating four-footed beasts after killing them,
and two-footed beings also who were there, brought in turn by Time. / In this way, a hundred years passed for him in that forest,
reproaching himself while devouring the flesh of beasts: / “When shall I again attain such a human condition?
I shall not commit this vile and great cause of taking birth in another species! / By hunting, running about out of greed for meat,
calamity has been attained, terrifying to humans; / painful to me is this sight of deer together with humans.
By sin I was reduced to wickedness, though born in a sinless family of the good; / I have been brought to deformity: behold the turn of Time!
Therefore there is no good deed for me, and injury alone is condemned; / by it sorrow is attained, and liberation will not come.
How will my liberation come to be? How can the doe's word prove true?” / When a hundred years had passed for him while living in that forest at that time,
a herd of cows arrived in due course for the sake of grass and water; / an enclosure of cowpens settled down, resting there,
and at the edge of the forest it was filled with the sound of churning-sticks; / that forest was also crowded with intoxicated cowherds and trees,
endowed with the sound of flutes at night, bringing auspiciousness to the gopīs. / Thus, while he was dwelling within the company of the Kharjūra forest,
there was a cow named Nandā, joyful, satisfied, and well-nourished, / the leader of the herd, swan-white in color, yielding jarfuls of milk,
with a long muzzle, well-proportioned limbs, beautiful limbs, thin hide, / a dark-colored throat, a fair neck, and sweet-sounding bells.
She grazed fearlessly ahead of the entire herd, / and going alone at her pleasure, she would graze in a hidden pasture.
Following her own desire, the gentle cow grazed on the hidden grass. / There, on the bank of the river, stood another mountain named Rohita,
Frequented by many creatures in its caverns, chasms, and caves. / In its northeastern region, terrifying and dense with grass,
Narrow, rugged, impassable, fearsome, and hair-raising, / teeming with deer and lions, frequented by many beasts of prey,
Dense with creepers, trees, and other growth, echoing with hundreds of jackals— / in this stronghold dwelt a fierce, terrifying [leopard], able to change form at will,
A leopard whose shoulders were smeared with blood, with terrible fangs and claws for weapons. / Meanwhile, the virtuous cowherd named Nanda, devoted to the welfare of his herd,
Was protecting his cattle with long, uncut grasses. / Having strayed from his herd through a desire for grass,
Grazing ahead, that cow arrived right before the tiger. / And the leopard rushed toward her, saying, 'Stop! Stop!
Today you are my appointed food; you have come of your own accord, O cow!' / Having heard the harsh, hair-raising words of the leopard,
That cow remembered her young, white-bodied, auspicious calf, / shining like the moon, and steeped in affection she spoke in a choked voice.
Burning with grief for her child, Nandā, loving her young, / wept piteously, despairing of ever seeing her child [again].
Seeing that cow crying and deeply distressed, / the leopard spoke terrifying words: 'O cow, why do you weep so much?
By fate you have come easily, food for me by chance. / Whether you weep or whether you laugh, your life has ended.
In this world one enjoys what is ordained; you have come of your own accord, O cow! / Your death is ordained this very day; why do you grieve in vain?'
The leopard asked her again, 'Why did you weep? / A great curiosity has arisen in me; tell me indeed.'
Hearing the tiger's words, Nandā then spoke these words: / 'You should forgive me, O lord! Salutations to you who can assume any form at will!
Once meeting you, there is no protection for any creature. / I do not grieve for my life; death must be met by me.
For to the born death is certain, and certain is birth to the dead; / therefore, I do not grieve over an inevitable matter, O king of beasts.
Just as even all the gods, powerless, must certainly die, / therefore, O tiger, I alone do not grieve for life.
Rather, O good one, I have wept out of affection and grief. / There is an anguish in my heart, and you ought to hear it.
In the first stage of youth, O king of beasts, I have given birth. / My first-born calf is a young boy, dear to me.
And my calf drinks only milk; even today he does not sniff grass. / He is tied in the cowherd's house, and tormented by hunger he looks for me.
I grieve for him: how will my child survive? / Overcome by love for my child, I wish to give him my breast.
Having suckled the calf at my breast and licked him on the head, / having entrusted him to my companions and instructed them on what is good and harmful,
I will return again, and you may eat me as you please.' / Hearing Nandā's words, the king of beasts spoke again:
'What is your child to do with you? Do you not understand death? / All living beings tremble and die upon beholding me,
Yet you, filled with pity, speak of "my child, my child"! / Neither sons, nor austerity, nor gifts, nor mother, nor father, nor teacher
Are able to protect a mortal oppressed by time. / How, having gone to Gokula crowded with cowherd women,
Resounding with bulls, heavenly, adorned with young calves, / an ornament of the world of the gods, equal to heaven without a doubt,
Ever joyful, celestial, worshiped by all the gods, / the pure among the pure, and the auspicious among the auspicious,
The sacred place of all sacred places, the most blessed among the blessed, / endowed with all virtues, the great abode of God,
Renowned above all sacred places, an unsurpassed heaven on earth, / [where] by the sound of the cowherdesses' churning and the lowing of young calves,
And by the lowing sound of cows, misfortune is repelled; / where calves moo piteously out of longing for their mothers,
Which is guarded by brave cowherds trained in hand-to-hand combat, / where songs, dances, and talk resound, filled with shouts of joy,
With calves standing here and there, bellowing on all sides, / the cow-pen shines like a lake with moving lotuses—
Having seen that gentle abode of Śrī, crowded with joyful and well-fed people, / resembling Goloka, how will you return?
O gentle one, let my five elements drink your blood! / I do not leave the elements despondent merely because of words.'
Nandā said: / 'O king of beasts, hear my words regarding one with her first calf: / having seen my companions, my young child, and the cowherds who protect us,
Having taken leave of the cowherd women and especially my mother, / I will return by oaths, if you agree to release me.
Whatever sin there is in killing a brāhmaṇa, or in slaying a mother or a father, / with that sin may I be tainted if I do not come back again!
Whatever sin belongs to hunters, to barbarians, and to poisoners, / with that sin may I be tainted if I do not come back again!
Those who would cause obstacles to cows and strike a sleeping cow— / with their sin may I be tainted if I do not come back again!
He who, having given a maiden once, wishes to give her to a second— / with his sin may I be tainted if I do not come back again!
That man who yokes unfit bullocks to a difficult [task], / or who causes an obstacle while a sacred tale is being recited—
With that sin may I be tainted if I do not come back again! / He from whose house a friend who has arrived departs disappointed—
With his sin may I be tainted if I do not come back again! / Through these terrible sins [if broken], I shall return again.'
Having gained confidence, the leopard spoke words again. / The tiger said: / 'Confidence has arisen in us, O cow, by your oaths.
Perhaps having gone there, you will think, "This fool has been deceived by me." / Even here some will say, "There is no sin in a [broken] oath
Toward passionate women, in marriages, and likewise in the release of cows, / or when loss of life has arisen"—you must not trust [them].
In this world there are certain atheists, fools who consider themselves scholars; / they will cause your mind to whirl in an instant like one mounted on a wheel.
Vile men, their minds veiled in ignorance through misleading arguments and reasons, / not skilled in the traditional scriptures, delude [others].
Very clever, they show even untruths as truths, / just as people skilled in the art of painting [show] depths and heights on a flat surface.
For the most part, once their purpose is accomplished, people do not think of their benefactor; / seeing the exhaustion of milk, a calf abandons its mother.
I do not see anyone in this world who repays a favor done. / For when his purpose has been fulfilled, everyone's mind turns elsewhere.
Oaths have been made mutually in the past by sages, gods, asuras, and mortals for the accomplishment of their ends; / we do not believe in them.'
Whoever curses even with truth in the presence of gods, fire, or elders, / King Vaivasvata cuts away half of his merit.
Do not let such a thought arise in your mind: “He was deceived by oaths.” / You have made everything visible yourself; do as you please now.
Nandā said: / “Just so, just so, O great good one! Who has the power to deceive you? / He alone deceives himself, who would deceive another.”
The leopard said: / “O little cow, loving toward your calf, go and see your little son. / Having suckled the calf at your udder and licked him on the head,
having seen your mother, your brother, your friends, and your kinsmen, / place truth at the very forefront, and return quickly.”
Having thus taken an oath, that cow who spoke truth, / permitted by the king of beasts, departed, loving toward her calf.
Her face filled with tears, miserable, trembling, greatly sorrowful, / uttering cries of “hambhā”, she fell into an ocean of grief.
Like an elephant seized by a crocodile's grip in a body of water, / powerless to protect herself, she lamented repeatedly.
She reached that cow-pen, situated on the bank of the river Hariṇī; / and hearing the calf crying, she ran out towards him.
Having approached that young one whose eyes were clouded with tears, / the calf, having reached his mother, asked her with apprehension:
“I see no calm in you; I do not perceive your courage today at all. / Your gaze is agitated, and you appear exceedingly terrified.”
Nandā said: / “Drink my udder today, my son, if you ask the reason. / I am unable to tell you; satisfy yourself as you desire.
This is the final seeing of your mother for you, my son, [now] hard to obtain. / Having drunk from me for this one day, whose [milk] will you drink tomorrow morning?
Leaving you behind, my son, I must go, for I came bound by oaths; / and my own life must be surrendered to the tiger emaciated by hunger.”
And having heard Nandā's words, the calf spoke this word. / The calf said: / “I will go to that place where you wish to go.
Death along with you is praiseworthy even for me, there is no doubt; / I would have to die all alone in agony without you.
If the tiger slays me together [with you] in the forest, O mother, / that destiny which belongs to those devoted to their mother will surely be mine.
Therefore, I shall certainly go with you, there is no doubt. / Or rather, mother, you stay: let your oaths be mine!
And what is the purpose of life for one separated from his mother? / For an orphan constantly in the forest, who will be my protector?
There is no kin equal to a mother for infants who live on milk; / there is no protector equal to a mother; there is no refuge equal to a mother.
There is no affection equal to a mother; there is no face equal to a mother; / there is no deity equal to a mother, both in this world and in the next.
Indeed, such is the supreme dharma fashioned by the Lord of Creatures; / the sons who always abide by this attain the supreme state.”
Nandā said: / “My death alone has been ordained, you shall not come, my son; / nor should there be the death of other living beings through the death of another.
This final, excellent message of a mother, my son: / stay here according to my word, and after that, [give] devotion again.
Roaming in water and on dry land, father, do not be heedless; / through heedlessness all beings perish, there is no doubt.
Nor should grass situated in dangerous places ever be grazed out of greed; / from greed comes the destruction of all, in this world and in the next.
Deluded by greed, my son, men enter the ocean and the wilderness; / through greed, even a learned person may commit an extremely fierce, wrongful act.
From greed, from heedlessness, from misplaced trust—through these three comes the ruin of men. / Therefore, one should not be greedy, one should not be heedless, one should not trust.
For the self must constantly be protected with effort, my son, / from all wild beasts and from perils such as barbarians and thieves.
Even among animals born of sinful wombs dwelling in one place, / the minds are unpredictable; know this, my little son.
Toward clawed creatures, rivers, horned beasts, those bearing weapons, / women, and servants, no trust should be placed by you.
One should not trust the untrustworthy, nor should one trust overly in the trustworthy; / fear born of misplaced trust cuts down even the roots.
One should not trust even one's own body, though strong, when the mind is afraid; / they will strike down secretly one who is sleeping, intoxicated, or through heedlessness.
Scent should constantly be smelled everywhere with effort; / cows see by scent, and kings by their spies' eyes.
One should not stay alone in a dreadful forest; one should contemplate dharma alone; / nor should distress be felt by you: death is certain for everyone.
Just as a traveller stays having taken shelter under the shade, / and having rested departs again, even so is the meeting of living beings.
My son, the entire world is impermanent; why do you alone grieve in it? / Meanwhile, having cast aside grief, follow my word.”
Having smelled that son on his head and licked him on his crown, / seized by great grief, her eyes confounded by tears,
sighing deeply and hotly again and again like a she-serpent, / she looked upon the world as though it were desolate without her son.
Standing like one plunged into deep mud and sinking, / lamenting, the cow Nandā spoke these words to her son once again:
“There is no affection equal to a son; there is no happiness equal to a son; / there is no delight equal to a son; there is no refuge equal to a son.
For the childless, the world is empty; for the childless, there is no happiness in the house; / through a son one attains the [heavenly] world; the childless goes to hell.
People speak the words: ‘Sandalwood, indeed, is cool’; / but the embrace of a son's body is cooler than sandalwood.”

Having thus recounted the virtues of her son and having gazed upon him again and again,
she urgently asked her mother, friends, and the cowherd women.
“As I was grazing at the head of the herd, the lord of beasts approached me; / I was released by him through oaths; I shall certainly go there again.
Having come by my truthful word to see my son, my mother, / my friends, and the cow-pen, I shall certainly go there again.
Mother, forgive all of that—bad behaviour and the like—done by me; / this little boy is your grandson; what else do I say in this matter?
O Vipulā, Campakā, mother Bhadrā, Surabhimāninī, / Vasudhārā, Priyānandā, Mahānandā, Ghaṭasravā!
Whatever unpleasant word was spoken either out of ignorance or knowingly, / forgive that, O noble ladies, and whatever else was done by me.
You who possess all virtues, who are the mothers of the whole world, / who constantly grant all things: protect my little boy!
Protect my little son, who is helpless, distressed, and wretched; / afflicted by grief for his mother, O sisters, you will nurture him.
Since you will protect this helpless, weak one like a son, / forgive me, O noble ladies; I shall depart relying on truth.
Nor should great anxiety be entertained in any way by you, my friends; / for one who has been born, death stands foremost.”
Hearing the words of Nandā, her mother and friends, sorrowful, / fell into extreme despondency, and astonished, spoke this:
“Ah, this is a great wonder, that you are prepared to fulfill / the dreadful word of the tiger! O Nandā, you are a speaker of truth!
Having averted great danger by oaths and true speech, / it must be destroyed with effort; one should not go [to death] in any way.
O Nandā, you must not go; adharma is committed by you, / since having abandoned your own young calf, you go out of longing for truth.
On this matter, a verse was spoken of old by sages who teach the Veda: / When the loss of life has arisen, there is no sin in oaths.
Where the protection of the life of living beings would occur by telling an untruth, / there untruth would be truth, and truth would even be untruth.
Regarding women, in marriages, likewise in the release of cows, / and in the misfortune of Brahmins, there is no sin in oaths.
Nandā said: / For the sake of protecting the lives of others, I would certainly speak an untrue word; / but for my own sake, for the sake of life, I do not dare speak [one] in any way.
Alone one is united in the womb, in death, and in maintenance; / and alone one experiences pleasure and pain. Therefore I speak the truth.
The worlds are established on truth; dharma is established on truth. / By the word of truth the ocean does not cross its boundary.
Having given the earth to Viṣṇu, Bali took refuge in Pātāla; / though bound by trickery, Bali did not abandon his word of truth.
The king of mountains, hundred-peaked, rising up as it expanded— / the Vindhya, standing by truth, does not overstep its bound.
Heaven, liberation, and hell are established on truthful speech; / but whoever violates speech, everything has been violated by him.
He who represents himself as other than he really is— / what sin has not been committed by him, a thief who steals himself?
I would go to a terrible hell by violating myself through myself; / King Vaivasvata cuts away half of that person’s dharma.
Having bathed in the deep, pure water of the pilgrimage of truth, the lake of forbearance, / freed from sin, one attains the supreme state.

A thousand horse sacrifices and truth were placed on a scale: / truth is indeed superior to a thousand horse sacrifices.

Truth is a noble fruit and the supreme scripture, free from affliction and the rest; / it is near to the virtuous, the family wealth of the good, the fruit of all stages of life.
Since having attained it one goes to heaven, how can it be abandoned? / O people gathered together here, speak truth daily, surely.
Her friends said: / O Nandā, you are to be saluted by all gods and demons alike, / you who, through supreme truthfulness, abandon life-breaths that are hard to abandon!
What shall we say there, O auspicious one, you who bear the burden of dharma? / By this renunciation, nothing whatever is unobtainable in the three worlds.
And we foresee non-separation from your son because of this renunciation; / for a woman whose mind is virtuous, there are no misfortunes anywhere.
Having seen all the cowherd women and circumambulated the cowpen, / Nandā departed, taking leave again of the gods and the trees:
The earth, Varuṇa, Agni, Vāyu, and also the Moon, / the deities of the ten directions, the trees, the constellations together with the planets—
she addressed them all, bowing down again and again: / 'Whatever siddhas and all forest deities have taken refuge in the forest,
let them protect my son wandering in the forest and [eating] grass! / O campaka, aśoka, punnāga, sarala, arjuna, and kiṃśuka trees,
let all trees hear my distressed message: / The calf is alone, wretched, wandering in the rugged forest;
protect the young calf out of affection, like a natural-born son! / Deprived of mother and father, lordless, dejected in mind,
wandering over this earth, weeping, very miserable— / for him weeping here in the great forest, my son,
overcome by great sorrow, afflicted by hunger and thirst, / desolated, alone, seeing the whole world as empty,
protection must be given as he wanders by those who have compassion.' / Having thus entrusted him with affection, overcome by maternal love for her son,
and ignited by the fire of grief, cut off from seeing her son, / like a separated she-cakravāka bird, like a creeper fallen from a tree,
like a blind woman lacking sight, stumbling at every step, / she went again to that place where that flesh-eater was.
He sat, his mouth gaping wide, sharp-fanged, terrifying. / Meanwhile, her son, the calf, with tail raised, very swift,
arrived before his mother and stood in front of the lord of beasts. / But having seen her son arrived, and death standing in front,
and having seen the tiger, the cow spoke these words: / 'O lord of beasts, here I have come, steadfast in the vow of the dharma of truth!
Satisfy yourself now as you desire with my flesh! / Satiate the spirits; drink my blood!
Only when I am dead, sir, may you devour this young calf.' / The leopard said: / 'Welcome to you, O auspicious one, O truthful cow!
Indeed, for the truthful nothing inauspicious happens anywhere. / You previously spoke the truth, O cow, about returning again;
thereby wonder has seized me: how could one who has reached [safety] come back? / You were sent back by me in order to test your truthfulness.
Otherwise, having reached [your] flesh, how would you go away alive? / And the wonder that arose in us was my quest for truth.
Therefore, by this truth, you are now released by me. / You are my sister, your son is my nephew.
Instruction has been given, O auspicious one, to me of most wicked deeds. / The worlds are established on truth; dharma is established on truth.
By truth the cow emits a stream of milk dear for oblations; / most blessed indeed is the cowherd who lives by your milk.
Blessed are those regions of earth and the grass-covered plants, O auspicious one! / They are blessed and have achieved their aim, and by them good deeds have been done;
the essence of life has been attained by those who drink your milk.' / Having acquired trust, the lord of beasts reached supreme wonder:
'This is an instruction for us; truth has been shown by the gods. / Having seen the beloved truth of cows, I have no desire to live.
Therefore I will do that deed by which I may be freed from guilt: / by me thousands and hundreds of living beings have been eaten.
What destination do I attain here, having seen such truth in a cow? / I am sinful, of bad conduct, cruel, a killer of living beings.
To what worlds shall I go, having done such terrible deeds? / I will go to holy pilgrimages; I will perform the purification of sin.
Having climbed a mountain I will jump down, or I will enter the fire. / O cow, what austerity must be performed by me today for purification from sin?
Direct that in brief, for this is not a time for elaboration.' / The cow said: / 'In the Kṛta age they praise austerity, and in the Tretā age knowledge;
in the Dvāpara age they say sacrifice, but in the Kali age gift alone. / Of all gifts whatsoever, this alone is the highest:
fearlessness to all beings; there is no gift higher than this. / He who bestows fearlessness to moving and unmoving beings,
freed from all fear, attains the supreme Brahman. / There is no gift equal to non-injury; there is no austerity equal to non-injury.
Just as in the footprints of an elephant every other footprint vanishes, / even so, O tiger, all dharmas vanish in non-injury.'
The shade of the tree of yoga destroys the three afflictions; / dharma and knowledge are its blossoms, and heaven and liberation are its fruits.”
The shade of the tree of yoga is recorded for one scorched by the three kinds of suffering; / having attained the highest extinction, one is not afflicted again by sufferings.
Thus this supreme good has been proclaimed to you in brief; / and everything is already known by you, yet you merely ask me.
The leopard said: / Formerly, cursed by a doe, I stood in the form of a tiger; / then, through the killing of living beings, all of it was entirely forgotten by me.
Through contact with you and your instruction, memory has arisen once again; / and you, through this truth, will also go to the highest state.
Therefore, I ask you again one question resting in my heart; / more than a hundred years have passed while I have been pondering it, O auspicious one.
By the conjunction of your good fortune, O fair one of heaven, somehow / an abode of dharma, established on the path of the virtuous, was made [by you].
What is your name, O auspicious lady of firm vows? Tell it to me, an ignorant one. / Nandā said: / My name Nandā was indeed given [to me] by my master Nanda.
Why were you standing [saying] 'I shall eat [you]' now? / Hearing that name 'Nandā', Prabhañjana was freed from the curse.
He attained kingship once again, endowed with strength and beauty. / In the meantime, Dharma, knowing that she spoke the truth,
arrived there to see [her] and addressed the milk-giving cow: / 'I, Dharma, have come here, delighted by your vow of truth.
O Nandā, choose a boon, may you be blessed—whatever is the most excellent boon.' / Addressed thus, indeed, that divine Nandā asked him for a boon:
'By your power, may I go together with my son to the highest abode, / and may this become an auspicious sacred place granting dharma to sages.
And by my name let this river be named the Nandā Sarasvatī, / through the granting of the boon, O lord of gods. That is what was requested by me.'
Pulastya said: / From that very moment, that divine one went to the auspicious abode of the truthful, / and Prabhañjana also reached that kingdom of his, acquired beforehand.
Since Nandā went to heaven having attained the delightful Sarasvatī, / by that name she has been called Nandā Sarasvatī by the wise.
The Sarasvatī, then, from that forest named Kharjūra, / went southwards again, flooding the surface of the earth.
A human who, even while approaching, utters her name, / obtains happiness while alive, and upon death becomes a sky-goer.
Those people of auspicious deeds who abandon their bodies there, / become kings of the vidyādharas, happy people.
The Sarasvatī is a ladder to heaven for mortals through bathing and drinking; / those who, well-composed, perform a bath there on the eighth lunar day,
having died and reached heaven, rejoice, exceedingly handsome. / The Sarasvatī there always grants marital bliss to women.
She who fasts on the third lunar day also becomes a recipient of marital bliss; / even by the sight of it there, one is freed from a collection of sins.
Whatever mortals touch it, they too should be known as foremost among sages; / by the gifting of silver, a mortal becomes endowed with beauty.
This holy river, endowed with sacred waters, is the daughter of Brahmā; / named Nandā, vast, she proceeded facing south.
Having gone not too far from there, she again turned away, facing backwards; / from that time on, that goddess remained visibly present by force.
On her sacred banks are sacred places and shrines / frequented on all sides by sages and also by siddhas.
At all of them, the great river Sarasvatī becomes a cause of dharma / through bathing, drinking, or the giving of gold.
The gift of gold, land, and cows given at the sacred place of Nandā by bathed men / yields great prosperity and generates an imperishable fruit.
Foremost sages proclaim the gift of grain to be praiseworthy, and likewise the gift of wealth; / that which is given by mortals at those sacred places has been taught as the foremost cause of dharma.
Whosoever, woman or man, self-controlled, should with effort fast to death there, / attaining union with the deity at those sacred places, he enjoys the fruit at will in the abode of Brahmā.

And those who die in her vicinity—both the immobile and the mobile—through the exhaustion of karma, / by all of them also the fruit of a sacrifice, difficult to attain, is forcefully and swiftly obtained.

Therefore, she grants the fruit of dharma to men whose minds are distressed by the sufferings of birth and so on; / with their whole soul, the Sarasvatī, yielding holy fruit, the great river, is to be resorted to with effort by mortals.
